description: We’re Zero Gravity, Zero Sleep, Information Systems students from Sunway University tackling Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots. We’re building a web app that turns 20+ years of NASA fire data into a burning calendar, inspired by the haze every Malaysian knows too well. We bring data analysis, dashboards and design. Looking for a web dev (React/Streamlit), someone handy with Python or stats, and anyone into Earth science. Curious and keen to learn? Message us!
summary: Burning Calendar is a web app that turns 26 years of NASA fire detections over Malaysia and Indonesia into one consistent record. NASA’s MODIS sensors have tracked fire hotspots since 2000, and VIIRS took over from 2012, but VIIRS picks up about five times as many hotspots in our region, so the two records cannot simply be joined. We scale the MODIS record into VIIRS-equivalent hotspots, then present the result as a burning calendar: pick an area and a period, and see when fires usually peak, which years were worst, and whether a given month is unusual. For a region that lives with haze almost every year, this gives responders, land managers and the public a fire history they can actually compare across decades.
details:
What it does

Burning Calendar lets a user choose an area of interest (a preset region such as Sumatra, Kalimantan or Peninsular Malaysia, or a custom latitude and longitude box) and any range of months from November 2000 to October 2026. It then shows:

  • a burning calendar of months by years, coloured by hotspot count or by how unusual each month was
  • a harmonisation check: scaled MODIS against real VIIRS for every month since 2012, for the chosen area
  • any chosen month compared with its historical median, the usual fire season, and the most unusual months
  • raw MODIS counts against the harmonised record
  • a map of where the hotspots were
  • downloads: the calendar, a yearly summary and the gridded hotspots (CSV), and the calendar as a picture

How it works

We downloaded about 8.2 million MODIS and VIIRS detections for Malaysia and Indonesia from NASA FIRMS: the yearly country files for 2000 to 2025, plus an archive request for January to October 2026. We removed low-confidence detections and non-vegetation sources such as volcanoes and gas flares, then counted hotspots per 0.25° grid cell, per month, separately for day and night. For 2012 to 2021, when both sensors were flying, we worked out how many VIIRS hotspots correspond to one MODIS hotspot for each 2° block. MODIS counts before February 2012 are multiplied by that factor. The final record joins scaled MODIS (November 2000 to January 2012), VIIRS S-NPP (to March 2018) and VIIRS NOAA-20 (April 2018 to October 2026). The two VIIRS satellites agree to within 1%.

How accurate it is

We tested the scaling on 2022 to 2025, years it had never seen. Yearly totals for the whole region were within 9% of the real VIIRS counts, and monthly totals within 13%. The record is reliable for islands, provinces and countries, but not for single 28 km cells. Quiet fire years are underestimated by roughly 10 to 25%, and November 2000 to July 2002 is less certain because only the Terra satellite was flying. August to October 2026 are near-real-time data in which volcanoes and gas flares could not be removed. The app states these limits on its method page and warns the user when the selected area is small.

Benefits and what we hope to achieve

The calendar makes patterns visible at a glance. September is the usual peak, and 2015 stands out as the worst year, with September 2015 at almost five times its usual level. The record also shows that 2026 is one of the worst fire seasons on record: October 2026 had 212,749 hotspots, 6.7 times a normal October, and only 2015 and 2006 were higher. Because MODIS is close to the end of its life, a VIIRS-based record that still reaches back to 2000 keeps that history usable. We hope to add daily updates from the FIRMS API, so responders can see a fire season building against 26 years of history and warn people before the haze arrives, and to extend the record to the rest of Southeast Asia.

Tools

Python (pandas, NumPy), Streamlit, Altair, pydeck, HTML and CSS, PowerShell, Google Colab, GitHub. Code: https://github.com/Fam-715/Burning-Calendar
